articles.title: Watch: Moment Esther Rantzen reunites man with children he saved from Nazi occupation
articles.summary: Sir Nicholas Winton's story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988.
articles.content:
Speaking in February 2024, Dame Esther said when she first got in touch with Sir Nicholas, who she called Nicky, she "congratulated him on his extraordinary achievement".

She told The Radio Times, external he had expressed some disappointment about his efforts, commenting that "not enough" people had been saved.

"I was devastated that he felt he had failed. I wanted to prove to this extraordinary man that every life he had saved was precious," Dame Esther added.

She invited him onto That's Life and during his first appearance, his scrapbook was shared with the audience, and two women he had saved as children - Vera Gissing and Lady Milena Grenfell-Baines - revealed their identities to him on TV.

They were sitting either side of Sir Nicholas, who had no idea of the surprise - something Dame Esther recalled as "incredibly moving".

Lady Milena is one of the most well-recognised Holocaust survivors in the UK.

She left Prague with her younger sister Eva at the age of nine, travelling on a special train arranged by Winton.

The two sisters were looked after by a Tameside family until their mother arrived the following year, having escaped via Norway.

Gissing, who was rescued from Prague in 1939 at the age of 11, lost most of her family during the Holocaust and ended up settling in the UK after the war ended.

"That was the only time in my career when I had to stop recording to wipe away my tears," Dame Esther also said.

The production team at That's Life were then contacted by several viewers who had watched the show and realised their connection to Sir Nicholas.

That gave the show's team an idea which would go on to become one of British television's most famous moments.

"In our next episode, I asked all those who owed their lives to him to stand, and Nicky, whom we had seated on the front row, turned to see the whole ground floor of the Television Theatre on their feet," Dame Esther recalled.

This story has broad historical and emotional significance, illustrating the value of every life saved and the enduring legacy of courageous human rights actions.
articles.personality_title: Sir Nicholas Winton reunited with children he saved during Nazi occupation on TV
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – During World War II, Sir Nicholas Winton helped save hundreds of children from Nazi-occupied Europe by arranging special trains to bring them to safety in the UK. For many years, his heroic actions were not widely known.

**What happened** – In February 1988, TV presenter Dame Esther Rantzen invited Sir Nicholas Winton onto the show That's Life!. During the show, two women he had rescued as children surprised him by revealing their identities on live television. Later, many others who owed their lives to him stood up in the audience, creating a powerful moment of reunion.

**Impact** – This event showed how one person's brave actions saved many lives and how important it is to remember and honor those efforts. It also helped Sir Nicholas realize that every life he saved was valuable, even though he once felt he had not done enough.

**What's next step** – The story brought more attention to Sir Nicholas Winton and the children he saved, inspiring others to learn about this history and the importance of helping people in danger.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A television reunion in 1988 brought Sir Nicholas Winton face-to-face with many of the children he saved from the Nazis, highlighting the lasting impact of his courage and kindness.

articles.title: Could a new global panel defuse inequality’s ‘ticking time bomb’?
articles.summary: What if the world tackled inequality with the same kind of scientific firepower it has brought to the climate crisis?
articles.content:
That is the thinking behind a proposal gaining support from world leaders and experts to establish a new ‘International Panel on Inequality’, an independent body that would bring together evidence on the causes and consequences of widening disparities and help governments understand what can be done about them.

The initiative was in the spotlight in New York on 23 September, at an event on the margins of the UN General Assembly’s high-level week, convened by Brazil, Norway, South Africa and Spain.

In remarks delivered by Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed, UN Secretary-General António Guterres cast the challenge in stark terms, warning of deepening concentrations of wealth and power and the risks they pose to societies and the international system.

“Sustainable Development Goal 10 calls on us to reduce inequality within and among nations. And yet we see breathtaking levels of income and wealth inequality, with the richest 10 per cent of the world’s population now owning 75 per cent of all wealth,” Mr. Guterres said.

When technology widens the divide

For the Secretary-General, the concern is not simply the scale of inequality today, but how quickly it could deepen.

He warned that the rapid development of frontier technologies could make existing disparities considerably worse, particularly if their wealth and power remain concentrated in only a few hands.

“The breakneck emergence of frontier technology – and the concentration of this technology’s wealth and power in a tiny number of hands – could unleash global inequality at a scale far beyond anything that we have seen,” he said.

The consequences, he warned, reach beyond household incomes and individual opportunity. Unchecked inequality could undermine democratic institutions and deepen the imbalance of power between countries.

“A world where only a few powerful countries can exert control over global security and the global economic architecture is a ticking time bomb,” he said.

Soundcloud

An IPCC for inequality?

According to the UN chief, the proposed International Panel on Inequality would seek to place independent, science-based evidence at the heart of the global response.

It would bring together experts to analyse the scale, causes and consequences of inequality and identify practical policy choices available to governments.

Those options could include greater investment in education, health, social protection and decent work; fairer taxation; stronger international cooperation on development finance, trade and investment; reform of the global financial architecture; and more effective enforcement of rules governing corporations and high-net-worth individuals operating across borders.

Gender equality would be central to the Panel’s work, alongside efforts to ensure that technologies such as artificial intelligence are accessible to, and governed by, all countries.

“This proposed Panel can deepen our understanding of the problem – and the policy and political choices that we need to address it,” the Secretary-General said.

‘A collective threat’

Nobel laureate economist Joseph Stiglitz, who chairs the founding committee behind the initiative, argued that inequality should be treated as a global challenge requiring the same depth of scientific analysis that climate change has received.

“Inequality within and between nations is a collective threat to the functioning of our economies and their ability to support human dignity,” he said, stressing that its effects extend well beyond economics to politics, societies and the environment.

The model is the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC, which provides the comparison at the heart of the initiative.

Mr. Stiglitz said the proposed inequality panel would similarly provide an independent body of experts able to “assess, synthesize, and present trusted knowledge and analysis” on the causes and consequences of inequality and possible policy responses.

But he also stressed the importance of giving such a body a multilateral foundation and legitimacy. The founding committee, he said, supports establishing the Panel through a UN resolution.

From proposal to UN resolution

Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley gave the proposal strong backing at the meeting, looking ahead to the possibility of action by the General Assembly.

For Ms. Mottley, tackling inequality goes to the heart of whether the international community can fulfil the promises made to people through the United Nations.

“I'd like to thank Brazil, Norway, South Africa, and Spain for convening this session that allows us to be able to tee up a resolution that I suspect will become a groundbreaking resolution for this body, recognizing that if we want to be able to guarantee the promise of the UN charter to our citizens across the world, it will be impossible for us to do without ensuring that we address this fundamental issue of income inequality,” said Ms. Mottley.

Watch the full meeting here.

articles.personality_title: World leaders propose new panel to study and reduce global inequality
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Inequality means that some people and countries have much more money and power than others. This gap is growing fast and could cause big problems for societies and governments around the world.

**What happened** – On September 23, during the United Nations General Assembly week, leaders from Brazil, Norway, South Africa, and Spain supported a plan to create an International Panel on Inequality. This group would collect and study facts about why inequality grows and suggest ways governments can reduce it. The idea is similar to the panel that studies climate change.

**Impact** – This panel would use science and expert advice to help countries make better decisions about issues like education, healthcare, taxes, and fair work. It could also help make sure new technologies like artificial intelligence benefit everyone, not just a few rich people. By understanding inequality better, the panel aims to protect democracy and keep power more balanced worldwide.

**What's next step** – The plan is to turn this idea into an official United Nations resolution. If approved, the panel would start working with experts from many countries to gather data and recommend policies. This could lead to stronger global cooperation to fight inequality.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new international panel is being proposed to study and tackle global inequality using science and expert advice, aiming to help governments create fairer societies.

articles.title: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
articles.summary: The social messaging app will let parents decide on privacy settings for their child's account.
articles.content:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children.

The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account.

In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.

And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness".

He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers.

"Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said.

"I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it."

The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries.

According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time.

The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls.

Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups.

Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content.

And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option.

"All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said.

The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms.

In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027.

It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media.

WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service.
articles.reasoning: WhatsApp's introduction of optional parental controls for teenagers represents a meaningful step toward enhancing child online safety and privacy. The controls empower parents to manage privacy settings without compromising message confidentiality, addressing growing concerns about children's digital wellbeing. This development has broad societal significance as it responds to regulatory pressures and aims to create safer online environments for minors globally. The article provides sufficient detail on the features and context, making it a substantive and positive change.
articles.personality_title: WhatsApp adds new parental controls to protect teen privacy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – WhatsApp, a popular messaging app, is responding to calls for safer online spaces for children. Governments and experts want tech companies to make their platforms more suitable and secure for young users.

**What happened** – WhatsApp introduced optional parental controls for teenagers. Parents can now manage privacy settings on their child's account, such as who can see their profile photo and who can add them to groups. Parents will also be notified when their teen joins or leaves a group. These controls do not allow parents to read their child's messages or calls, which stay private thanks to encryption. The controls can be turned on or off by parents using a special PIN.

**Impact** – This is an important step because it helps parents protect their teenagers online while respecting their privacy. It gives families more control without exposing private conversations. WhatsApp also includes settings for how teens use features like Channels and its AI assistant, which helps keep content appropriate. This approach balances safety with privacy better than some previous solutions.

**What's next step** – The new controls will be available soon, and parents can decide if they want to use them. Governments are still working on rules for online safety, including age checks for social media users. WhatsApp will continue to update its tools based on feedback and regulations to improve child safety.

**One-sentence takeaway** – WhatsApp’s new parental controls offer families a way to protect teens online while keeping their messages private and secure.
articles.personality_title_fr: WhatsApp lance de nouveaux contrôles parentaux pour protéger la vie privée des adolescents
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – WhatsApp, une application de messagerie populaire, répond aux demandes pour des espaces en ligne plus sûrs pour les enfants. Les gouvernements et les experts veulent que les entreprises technologiques rendent leurs plateformes plus adaptées et sécurisées pour les jeunes utilisateurs.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – WhatsApp a introduit des contrôles parentaux optionnels pour les adolescents. Les parents peuvent désormais gérer les paramètres de confidentialité du compte de leur enfant, comme qui peut voir leur photo de profil et qui peut les ajouter à des groupes. Les parents seront aussi informés lorsque leur adolescent rejoint ou quitte un groupe. Ces contrôles ne permettent pas aux parents de lire les messages ou appels de leur enfant, qui restent privés grâce au chiffrement. Les contrôles peuvent être activés ou désactivés par les parents avec un code PIN spécial.

**Impact** – C’est une étape importante car elle aide les parents à protéger leurs adolescents en ligne tout en respectant leur vie privée. Elle donne plus de contrôle aux familles sans exposer les conversations privées. WhatsApp inclut aussi des réglages pour l’utilisation des fonctionnalités comme les Channels et son assistant IA, ce qui aide à garder un contenu adapté. Cette approche équilibre mieux la sécurité et la vie privée que certaines solutions précédentes.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les nouveaux contrôles seront bientôt disponibles, et les parents pourront choisir de les utiliser ou non. Les gouvernements travaillent encore sur des règles pour la sécurité en ligne, y compris des vérifications d’âge pour les utilisateurs des réseaux sociaux. WhatsApp continuera de mettre à jour ses outils selon les retours et les règles pour améliorer la sécurité des enfants.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les nouveaux contrôles parentaux de WhatsApp offrent aux familles un moyen de protéger les adolescents en ligne tout en gardant leurs messages privés et sécurisés.
articles.personality_title_es: WhatsApp añade nuevos controles parentales para proteger la privacidad de los adolescentes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – WhatsApp, una aplicación de mensajería popular, está respondiendo a las demandas de espacios en línea más seguros para los niños. Los gobiernos y expertos quieren que las empresas tecnológicas hagan sus plataformas más adecuadas y seguras para los usuarios jóvenes.

**Qué pasó** – WhatsApp introdujo controles parentales opcionales para adolescentes. Los padres ahora pueden gestionar la configuración de privacidad en la cuenta de su hijo, como quién puede ver su foto de perfil y quién puede agregarlos a grupos. También recibirán avisos cuando su hijo se una o salga de un grupo. Estos controles no permiten a los padres leer los mensajes o llamadas de sus hijos, que permanecen privados gracias al cifrado. Los controles pueden activarse o desactivarse con un PIN especial que pone el padre.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque ayuda a los padres a proteger a sus adolescentes en línea respetando su privacidad. Da más control a las familias sin exponer las conversaciones privadas. WhatsApp también incluye configuraciones para el uso que hacen los adolescentes de funciones como Channels y su asistente de inteligencia artificial, lo que ayuda a mantener contenido apropiado. Este enfoque equilibra mejor la seguridad y la privacidad que algunas soluciones anteriores.

**Próximo paso** – Los nuevos controles estarán disponibles pronto y los padres podrán decidir si los usan. Los gobiernos siguen trabajando en reglas para la seguridad en línea, incluyendo verificaciones de edad para usuarios de redes sociales. WhatsApp continuará actualizando sus herramientas según los comentarios y regulaciones para mejorar la seguridad infantil.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Los nuevos controles parentales de WhatsApp ofrecen a las familias una forma de proteger a los adolescentes en línea mientras mantienen sus mensajes privados y seguros.
